Indian and international evidence independently demonstrates that delayed notification, provider identification and acknowledgement failures can create patient-safety risk and human escalation work. [Panacea Journal — Critical Value Analysis at Fortis Multispeciality Hospital, Bangalore](https://newp.pjms.in/index.php/pjms/article/view/817)

**Evidence:** 75,156 tests; 2,199 critical values; emergency 55.7%; SMS + telephone; SMS failure fallback; read-back and call logging.

### E-002 — Indian Critical-Value Notification Study

[PubMed — Variables Affecting Critical Value Notification](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25646047/)

**Evidence:** 1,187 critical values; 64.61% notified 30–120 minutes after sample receipt; caregiver identification/contact difficulties.

### E-003 — Indian Quality Improvement

[PMC — Quality Tools and Strategy for Critical Alerts](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9763056/)

**Evidence:** delayed/failed notification and process/root-cause analysis in Delhi tertiary hospital.

### E-004 — Delay Root Causes

[Oxford Academic — Quality Improvement in Critical Value Delivery](https://academic.oup.com/jalm/article/6/4/985/6255453)

**Evidence:** underused escalation protocols, delayed calls and difficulty identifying/contacting providers.

### E-005 — Closed-Loop Communication

[PMC — Provider-Team Smartphone Critical-Result Communication](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8442100/)

**Evidence:** difficulty identifying appropriate providers and obtaining timely acknowledgement; smartphone workflow substantially improved successful notification.

### E-006 — Computerized Notification

[PubMed — Computerized Critical-Value Notification](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19228648/)

**Evidence:** automated communication improved notification timeliness and likelihood of reaching physicians.

### E-007 — Push Notification Efficiency

[PubMed — Push Notifications for Critical Lab Results](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37600076/)

**Evidence:** electronic acknowledgement saved laboratory technicians an average of 10 minutes per acknowledged result compared with existing workflow.

hypotheses.statement:
The strongest ART surface is:

```text
CRITICAL RESULT
      ↓
CREATE SAFETY EXCEPTION
      ↓
IDENTIFY RESPONSIBLE TEAM
      ↓
SEND ALERT
      ↓
TRACK DELIVERY
      ↓
TRACK ACKNOWLEDGEMENT
      ↓
NO ACKNOWLEDGEMENT?
      ↓
AGE
      ↓
ESCALATE
      ↓
SECONDARY OWNER
      ↓
ACKNOWLEDGEMENT
      ↓
AUDIT / CLOSE
```

ART should not:

- interpret the laboratory result;
- determine treatment;
- override clinical judgement;
- prescribe;
- decide whether the result is clinically critical.

ART's potential role is **closed-loop communication and escalation**.

---

The addressable unit should be:

> **unresolved critical-result exception**

rather than:

> **critical-result notification**

Potential value components:

```text
1. FOLLOW-UP TIME
2. ESCALATION TIME
3. LABORATORIAN INTERRUPTION
4. DELAY REDUCTION
5. CLOSURE VISIBILITY
6. AUDIT / QUALITY WORK
7. POTENTIAL SAFETY-RISK REDUCTION
```

Only **1–3** can currently be reasonably modelled with external time evidence.

**4–7 require primary hospital evidence before quantification.**

**Industry:** Healthcare / Hospital Operations  
**Company:** Fortis Healthcare — Bengaluru  
**Candidate mid-scale site:** Fortis Hospital CG Road, Bengaluru  
**Workflow:** Critical Laboratory Result Notification + Closed-Loop Acknowledgement  
**Pain type:** Patient Safety / Time-Critical Clinical Communication  
**VRL checkpoint:** OPP-012-01  
**Decision:** **PASS → High-consequence, repeatable workflow target**

---

This discovery deliberately targets a workflow where:

> **a clinically dangerous laboratory result exists, someone must be reached quickly, acknowledgement must occur, and failure to close the communication loop creates patient-safety exposure.**

This is materially stronger than ordinary administrative automation.

The opportunity is not:

> “automate laboratory reporting.”

It is:

> **automate the unresolved exception between critical-result generation and verified clinical acknowledgement.**

---

Fortis Healthcare operates multiple Bengaluru hospitals. Its official site lists **Fortis Hospital CG Road, Bengaluru** as a **119-bed NABH-accredited hospital with 36 ICU beds and 8 HDU beds**, making it a relevant mid-scale hospital candidate. [Official Fortis Hospital CG Road](https://www.fortishealthcare.com/location/fortis-hospital-cg-road-bangalore)

**Important evidence boundary:** the published critical-value study used below identifies the study site only as a **Fortis multispeciality hospital, Bangalore**. It does not explicitly identify the branch as CG Road. Therefore, the 119-bed CG Road figure is used only to establish a **mid-scale Fortis Bengaluru candidate**, not to falsely attribute the study's laboratory numbers to that exact branch.

---

A peer-reviewed 2022 study was conducted in the laboratory of a **Fortis multispeciality hospital, Bangalore**, over January 2020–June 2021.

The laboratory processed:

- **75,156 tests**
- **2,199 critical values**
- **1,224 critical values (55.7%) from emergency**
- **900 (40.9%) from inpatient departments**
- **75 (3.4%) from outpatient departments**

Creatinine accounted for **1,151 (52.3%)** of the critical values.

[Panacea Journal of Medical Sciences — Fortis Bengaluru Critical Value Study](https://newp.pjms.in/index.php/pjms/article/view/817)

The study explicitly states that critical values require immediate communication and that both telephone and SMS notification were used.

---

The published Fortis Bengaluru study describes this process:

```text
TEST RESULT
    ↓
CRITICAL RANGE DETECTED
    ↓
RESULT VALIDATED
    ↓
RESPONSIBLE CAREGIVER IDENTIFIED
    ↓
TELEPHONE NOTIFICATION
    +
SMS NOTIFICATION
    ↓
READ-BACK
    ↓
CRITICAL VALUE LOG
```

The laboratory also checked whether the SMS was forwarded. If it failed, the technologist manually notified the caregiver by telephone and entered the details into the critical-call log.

[Fortis Bengaluru Critical Value Study](https://newp.pjms.in/index.php/pjms/article/view/817)

This is extremely important for ART:

> **A failure state already exists inside the published workflow.**

---

The normal workflow is:

```text
CRITICAL RESULT
      ↓
AUTOMATED / STANDARD NOTIFICATION
      ↓
CAREGIVER RECEIVES
      ↓
ACKNOWLEDGES
      ↓
CLINICAL ACTION
```

The exception is:

```text
CRITICAL RESULT
      ↓
NOTIFICATION ATTEMPT
      ↓
NO DELIVERY / NO RESPONSE / WRONG RECIPIENT
      ↓
HUMAN INTERVENTION
      ↓
PHONE / SECONDARY CONTACT
      ↓
READ-BACK
      ↓
DOCUMENT
      ↓
CLOSE
```

The Fortis study explicitly reports SMS failure followed by manual telephone notification.

---

A critical laboratory value represents a result requiring immediate communication because it may indicate a life-threatening state requiring prompt action.

Indian laboratory research identifies failure to notify the responsible caregiver in a timely manner as a patient-safety issue that may contribute to diagnostic error.

[Study of Variables Affecting Critical Value Notification — PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25646047/)

That study analysed **1,187 critical values** and found that **64.61% of critical values were notified between 30 and 120 minutes after sample receipt**. It identified difficulty contacting the responsible caregiver and incomplete information about the treating physician/location among important concerns.

---

The key insight is that:

> **Sending the alert is not the same as completing the communication.**

A critical-result workflow needs:

```text
SEND
 ↓
DELIVER
 ↓
RECEIVE
 ↓
ACKNOWLEDGE
 ↓
ESCALATE IF NOT ACKNOWLEDGED
 ↓
VERIFY
 ↓
CLOSE
```

A 360-bed paediatric hospital study found that timely outgoing notification was >90%, but timely clinician acknowledgement for one high-risk service was **<5%** before intervention. The hospital identified difficulty identifying the correct provider and achieving closed-loop communication as key drivers.

[Closed-loop communication using provider-team smartphones — PMC](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8442100/)

This is powerful evidence that:

> **the residual problem can exist after the alert has already been sent.**

A computerized critical-value notification study found automated communication improved notification timeliness and increased the likelihood of reaching the physician on call.

[Evaluation of computerized notification system — PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19228648/)

A later ICU pilot using push notifications reported that each electronic acknowledgement saved laboratory technicians an average of **10 minutes** compared with the existing workflow.

[Push notifications for critical lab results — PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37600076/)

This does not prove ART is required.

It proves that **communication automation can materially improve this workflow**, making the problem commercially interesting.

ART should not:

- determine treatment;
- override clinical judgement;
- prescribe;

ART's potential role is **closed-loop communication and escalation**.

The same workflow appears wherever a healthcare organisation must communicate a time-critical exception:

```text
LAB
→ CRITICAL RESULT

RADIOLOGY
→ CRITICAL / UNEXPECTED FINDING

PHARMACY
→ HIGH-RISK MEDICATION EXCEPTION

ICU
→ DETERIORATION ALERT

BLOOD BANK
→ TRANSFUSION SAFETY EXCEPTION
```

The underlying automation primitive is:

> **event → responsible owner → acknowledgement → ageing → escalation → closure**

Therefore the eventual ART product opportunity could be broader than laboratory alerts.

> **When a critical laboratory result cannot be successfully communicated and acknowledged through the normal notification path, what human investigation, fallback communication and escalation work is required before the case can close?**

The Fortis Bengaluru study documents a critical-value workflow using telephone notification, SMS notification and read-back. It also identifies the workflow as a patient-safety process requiring immediate communication.

The published study does not provide a complete modern closed-loop escalation design for the hospital.

Therefore this reconstruction separates:

- **Fortis Bengaluru evidence**
- **general critical-value workflow evidence**
- **reconstructed exception path**

---

The published study covered:

```text
75,156 TESTS
      ↓
2,199 CRITICAL VALUES
      ↓
EMERGENCY 55.7%
INPATIENT 40.9%
OUTPATIENT 3.4%
```

The laboratory used:

- telephone communication;
- SMS communication;
- read-back for telephone notification.

The study reports that SMS critical-alert send-outs helped reduce critical-value turnaround time.

---

The evidence-supported normal path is:

```text
CRITICAL RESULT GENERATED
        ↓
RESULT VERIFIED
        ↓
RESPONSIBLE CAREGIVER IDENTIFIED
        ↓
TELEPHONE + / OR SMS
        ↓
READ-BACK / RECEIPT
        ↓
DOCUMENT
        ↓
CLINICAL RESPONSE
        ↓
CLOSE
```

The Fortis study explicitly identifies critical-value notification as immediate communication and reports use of both verbal and SMS notification plus read-back.

---

The first exception is:

```text
CRITICAL RESULT
      ↓
NORMAL NOTIFICATION
      ↓
FAILURE
```

Possible failure states supported by the broader evidence include:

- responsible clinician cannot be identified;
- clinician cannot be reached;
- notification is delayed;
- acknowledgement does not occur;
- the initial communication path fails.

A paediatric hospital study found that timely outgoing notification exceeded 90%, while timely clinician acknowledgement was below 5% for one high-volume inpatient service; process analysis identified difficulty identifying appropriate clinicians and achieving closed-loop communication.

---

The Fortis Bengaluru study establishes the use of SMS alongside telephone communication.

The broader closed-loop model demonstrates why an electronic send is insufficient:

```text
SEND
 ↓
DELIVERY
 ↓
ACKNOWLEDGEMENT
```

These are separate states.

A system may successfully send a message while still failing to establish that the responsible clinician has received and acknowledged the result.

Therefore the automation question is not:

> “Was the SMS sent?”

It is:

> **“Has an authorised caregiver acknowledged responsibility for the critical result?”**
